justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I understood to be the prevailing S&P 500 level at the time of the forecast, sitting in the low-to-mid 3000s. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the most recent closing price, expecting minimal movement absent a major catalyst, which is consistent with the empirical observation that daily index returns are small relative to the level. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the figure slightly higher to reflect a modest positive drift assumption embedded in equity markets over short periods, while acknowledging that a week introduces meaningfully more variability. For the one-month horizon, the point estimate continues that gentle upward drift, reflecting the historical tendency for equities to trend higher over time, though at this horizon the range of plausible outcomes widens considerably.

The confidence interval widths are calibrated primarily to realized volatility in the S&P 500. Daily implied and historical volatility in the S&P 500 typically runs somewhere in the range of 15–25% annualized, which translates to roughly 1–1.5% daily moves at one standard deviation. For the one-day window, this produces a fairly tight band, while the one-week and one-month intervals expand in proportion to the square root of time, following standard diffusion logic. I also allowed for some additional uncertainty beyond pure statistical volatility, recognizing that discrete news events — earnings, macro data releases, central bank communications — can produce non-normal return distributions with fat tails.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sharp deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift toward tighter conditions, or a geopolitical shock could easily produce moves of 5–10% or more, breaching the lower bounds of even the one-month interval. Credit market stress or a liquidity event — similar in character to what occurred in March 2020 or late 2018 — could produce far larger drawdowns. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot from the Fed, a significant de-escalation in geopolitical tensions, or an unexpectedly strong earnings season could drive a sharp rally. My intervals are explicitly not designed to capture these tail scenarios with high probability; they represent the central 90% of outcomes under relatively normal market functioning, and true fat-tail events remain a meaningful residual risk outside those bounds.
